questions.q: What are the three kinds of incentives the authors describe?
a: Economic, social and moral
Financial, legal and personal
Positive, negative and neutral
Individual, group and cultural
questions.why: The first lesson separates incentives into money and time, reputation among peers, and conscience.

questions.q: What happens when you combine several kinds of incentives?
a: The incentive becomes more powerful
They cancel each other out
Only the economic one still matters
People stop noticing any of them
questions.why: The summary says the criminal penalty for a crime works because it stacks economic, moral and social costs.

questions.q: Why might a real estate agent push you to accept an offer quickly?
a: A fast sale earns her more per hour than waiting
She is legally required to close within a month
She earns the same flat fee whatever the price
She wants to spare you the stress of waiting
questions.why: The second lesson does the commission math: a higher price takes longer and can pay her less overall.

questions.q: What do studies show about agents who sell their own houses?
a: They wait longer and get higher prices
They accept the first offer to save time
They price lower so the sale is quick
They refuse to use other agents at all
questions.why: The second lesson uses this contrast to show how information asymmetry lets experts profit from a fast sale.

questions.q: What does the summary conclude about campaign spending and election results?
a: Money correlates with winning but does not cause it
Spending is the strongest cause of victory
Voters pay no attention to spending at all
Spending only matters in close races
questions.why: The third lesson says candidates could halve their budgets and lose about 1% of voters, so correlation is not causation.
